content:
This is the classic “trolley problem.” There is no single universally agreed answer, but the two main ethical approaches give different responses.

1) Utilitarian / consequentialist answer
- Act to produce the best overall outcome: pull the lever. Five lives saved vs. one lost — net harm is minimized. From this view, consequences (lives saved) are what matter, so diverting the trolley is the right thing.

2) Deontological / rights-based answer
- Morally wrong to intentionally kill an innocent person even to save more lives. Pulling the lever makes you an agent who causes the single person’s death; letting things stand is an omission. On this view, you should not pull the lever because actively killing is impermissible, even if it reduces total deaths.

Other considerations that complicate the simple framing
- Intention vs. foresight: Some argue it’s acceptable to foreseen but unintended harm (diversion) to save many, but not to intend harm as a means to an end.
- Responsibility: Some feel a moral difference between doing harm and allowing harm, though many philosophers challenge that distinction.
- Credibility/uncertainty: If you’re uncertain (maybe the switch fails, the one person is a child/guardian, etc.) that changes the calculus.
- Emotions and moral psychology: People’s intuitions vary; emotional aversion to being the direct agent of a death is powerful.

Practical conclusion
If you adopt a consequentialist stance (most common practical ethicists, emergency responders, and utilitarians), pull the lever to minimize total loss of life. If you’re guided by a strict deontological rule against intentionally killing, do nothing. In real-world decisions, the minimizing-harm rationale (pull the lever) is generally the more compelling and actionable answer: you save four additional lives at the cost of one.
